summary: Defines a way for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 routers to advertise optional capabilities to others in the routing domain using a new Router Information LSA. It can be flooded at link, area, or AS scope. It was replaced by RFC 7770.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers hold up a card listing the special things they can do so other routers know what to ask of them. A newer RFC replaced this.

questions: how do ospf routers advertise capabilities
what is the router information lsa
subtitle: Router Information LSA for advertising OSPF router capabilities.

tldr.problem: In OSPF, all bits in the options field are allocated, so new router capabilities cannot be advertised within the existing protocol.
tldr.mechanism: Defines a new Router Information (RI) Link State Advertisement that routers can use to advertise optional capabilities via TLVs (Type-Length-Value fields) that can be flooded at link, area, or AS scope.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now advertise their optional capabilities informally to enable capability discovery and advertisement. It was replaced by RFC 7770.

facts.label: Reserved SPI range for new TLVs

today: RFC 7770 updated this specification to extend OSPF for advertising optional router capabilities.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF routers currently advertise their capabilities using the options field in LSAs and hello packets. However, in OSPFv2, all bits in this field have been allocated, leaving no space for new capability advertisements. OSPFv3 has more room but benefits from a unified mechanism. This RFC solves the problem by introducing a new Router Information (RI) LSA that carries router capabilities in flexible Type-Length-Value (TLV) format.

For existing OSPF capabilities, this advertisement is informational in nature. For future OSPF extensions, the RI LSA can serve as the primary mechanism for advertising and discovering new features.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers have a bulletin board where they announce what they can do. The old bulletin board is full. This adds a new expandable bulletin board that can hold announcements about any new ability a router gains.

sections.title: Router Information LSA Format
sections.content:
In OSPFv2, the RI LSA is implemented as an Opaque LSA with type 4 and opaque ID 0, using link-scoped (type 9), area-scoped (type 10), or AS-scoped (type 11) flooding. In OSPFv3, it uses LSA function code 12 with the U bit set, allowing flooding even if the LSA type is not understood.

The payload of an RI LSA consists of one or more TLV triplets. Each TLV has a 16-bit Type field, a 16-bit Length field (in octets), and a variable-length Value. TLVs are padded to 4-octet alignment. The first TLV is typically the Router Informational Capabilities TLV (Type 1), which contains a 32-bit informational capability field where each bit represents a supported capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a container with labeled sections inside (TLVs). Each section says what kind of information it is and how long it is. The first section lists which special abilities the router has, using 32 on/off switches (bits).

sections.title: Capability Bits and Advertisement Scope
sections.content:
The RFC defines six assigned capability bits (bits 0 through 5): OSPF graceful restart capable, OSPF graceful restart helper, OSPF Stub Router support, OSPF Traffic Engineering support, OSPF point-to-point over LAN, and OSPF Experimental TE. Bits 6-31 are unassigned and available for future use via Standards Action.

A router MAY advertise different capabilities at different flooding scopes. For example, a router might support Traffic Engineering domain-wide but only in some attached areas. A router MAY originate its first RI LSA when the OSPF instance is created and updates it whenever a capability is configured or changed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each bit in the capability field means the router can do something special: restart gracefully, work as a stub router, handle traffic engineering, etc. A router can have different abilities at different scopes (just in one area versus the whole network).

sections.title: Extensibility and TLV Design
sections.content:
The RI LSA is designed to be a generic container for aggregate router information, not a catch-all for any information. TLVs have a single value or very few values to keep the RI LSA size small so it fits in a single LSA. Future specifications MUST explicitly state whether a new TLV applies to OSPFv2 only, OSPFv3 only, or both. The Router Informational Capabilities TLV is the first TLV and is followed by optional TLVs that specify details about capabilities.

New RI LSA TLVs are assigned through Standards Action in the range 2-32767. Experimental TLVs use the range 32768-32777, and the range 32778-65535 is reserved for future standardization.
sections.plainLanguage: The RI LSA is expandable: new features can add new sections (TLVs) to describe themselves in detail. But it is not a dumping ground for random data; each new feature must be carefully specified and approved.

sections.title: Security and Deployment Considerations
sections.content: The Router Informational Capabilities TLV is less critical than the topology information advertised by the base OSPF protocol. The informational capabilities have no impact on OSPF protocol operation—they are purely informational. Security considerations for future TLVs depend on the application and MUST be described when new capabilities are proposed. The base OSPF protocol security considerations apply, including OSPF authentication mechanisms that protect LSA flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: These capability announcements are informational; they do not directly control routing. Routers can ignore them if they want. The main OSPF security (authentication of routing messages) still applies to protect the RI LSA.
